The <hi type="italic">Onom.</hi> (<hi type="italic">s. v.</hi> <hi type="italic">Achsaph</hi>) says nothing more about its situation than that it was <hi type="italic">in tribu Aser</hi>, whilst the statement made <hi type="italic">s. v.</hi> <hi type="italic">Acsaph</hi> (Ἀκσάφ), that it was <hi type="italic">villula Chasalus</hi> (κώμη Ἐξάδους), eight Roman miles from Diocaesarea <hi type="italic">ad radicem montis Thabor</hi>, leads into the territory of Zebulun.
entries.19aecbc7b0a279f6f50b77cbfd33b946d42d43fc: <reference osisRef="Josh.19.26">Jos 19:26</reference> <hi type="italic">Alammalech</hi> has been preserved, so far as the name is concerned, in the Wady <hi type="italic">Malek</hi> or <hi type="italic">Malik</hi> (<hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> Bibl. Res. p. 110), which runs into the Kishon, since in all probability the wady was named after a place either near it or within it. <hi type="italic">Amad</hi> is supposed by <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> to be the present <hi type="italic">Haifa</hi>, about three hours to the south of Acre, on the sea, and this he identifies with the sycamore city mentioned by <hi type="italic">Strabo</hi> (xvi. 758), <hi type="italic">Ptolemy</hi> (v. 15, 5), and <hi type="italic">Pliny</hi> (h. n. v. 17), which was called <hi type="italic">Epha</hi> in the time of the Fathers (see <hi type="italic">Ritter</hi>, Erdk. xvi. pp. 722ff.). In support of this he adduces the fact that the Hebrew name resembles the Arabic noun for sycamore-an argument the weakness of which does not need to be pointed out. <hi type="italic">Misheal</hi> was assigned to the Levites (<reference osisRef="Josh.21.30">Jos 21:30</reference>, and <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.74">1Ch 6:74</reference>, where it is called <hi type="italic">Mashal</hi>). According to the <hi type="italic">Onom.</hi> (<hi type="italic">s. v.</hi> <hi type="italic">Masan</hi>) it was on the sea-coast near to Carmel, which is in harmony with the next clause, “<hi type="italic">and reacheth to Carmel westwards, and to Shihor-libnath</hi>.” <hi type="italic">Carmel</hi> (i.e., fruit-field), which has acquired celebrity from the history of Elijah (1Ki 18:17.), is a wooded mountain ridge which stretches in a north-westerly direction on the southern side of the Kishon, and projects as a promontory into the sea. Its name, “fruit-field,” is well chosen; for whilst the lower part is covered with laurels and olive trees, the upper abounds in figs and oaks, and the whole mountain is full of the most beautiful flowers. There are also many caves about it (vid., <hi type="italic">v. Raumer</hi>, Pal. pp. 43ff.; and <hi type="italic">Ritter</hi>, Erdk. xvi. pp. 705-6). The <hi type="italic">Shihor-libnath</hi> is not the <hi type="italic">Belus</hi>, or glass-river, in the neighbourhood of Acre, but is to be sought for on the south of Carmel, where Asher was bounded by Manasseh (<reference osisRef="Josh.17.10">Jos 17:10</reference>), i.e., to the south of Dor, which the Manassites received in the territory of Asher (<reference osisRef="Josh.17.11">Jos 17:11</reference>); it is therefore in all probability the <hi type="italic">Nahr Zerka</hi>, possibly the crocodile river of <hi type="italic">Pliny</hi> (<hi type="italic">Reland</hi>, Pal. p. 730), which is three hours to the south of Dor, and whose name (<hi type="italic">blue</hi>) might answer both to <hi type="italic">shihor</hi> (black) and <hi type="italic">libnath</hi> (white).
entries.33c1f056625360fc4c19f2de7edfb2a8015c4829: <reference osisRef="Josh.19.27">Jos 19:27</reference> <div eID="gen2943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2944" type="x-p"/> From this point the boundary “<hi type="italic">turned towards the east</hi>,” probably following the river <hi type="italic">Libnath</hi> for a short distance upwards, “<hi type="italic">to Beth-dagon</hi>,” which has not yet been discovered, and must not be identified with Beit Dejan between Yafa and Ludd (Diospolis), “<hi type="italic">and touched Zebulun and the valley of Jiphtah-el on the north of Beth-emek, and Nehiël, and went out on the left of Cabul</hi>,” i.e., on the northern side of it. The north-west boundary went from Zebulun into the valley of <hi type="italic">Jiphtah-el</hi>, i.e., the upper part of the Wady <hi type="italic">Abilîn</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.14">Jos 19:14</reference>). Here therefore the eastern boundary of Asher, which ran northwards from Wady Zerka past the western side of Issachar and Zebulun, touched the north-west corner of Zebulun. The two places, <hi type="italic">Beth-emek</hi> and <hi type="italic">Nehiël</hi> (the latter possibly the same as <hi type="italic">Neah</hi> in <reference osisRef="Josh.19.13">Jos 19:13</reference>), which were situated at the south of the valley of Jiphtah-el, have not been discovered; they may, however, have been upon the border of Zebulun and yet have belonged to Ashwer. <hi type="italic">Cabul</hi>, the κώμη Χαβωλώ of <hi type="italic">Josephus</hi> (Vit. §43), in the district of Ptolemais, has been preserved in the village of <hi type="italic">Kabul</hi>, four hours to the south-east of Acre (<hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> Bibl. Res. p. 88, and <hi type="italic">Van de Velde</hi>, R. i. p. 218).
entries.97441b07bc718f44f2a2adc7d6630739d7b8aadc: <reference osisRef="Josh.19.28-Josh.19.30">Jos 19:28-30</reference> <div eID="gen2944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2945" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Josh.19.28-Josh.19.30">Jos 19:28-30</reference> the towns and boundaries in the northern part of the territory of Asher, on the Phoenician frontier, are given, and the Phoenician cities Sidon, Tyre, and Achzib are mentioned as marking the boundary. First of all we have four towns in <reference osisRef="Josh.19.28">Jos 19:28</reference>, reaching as far as Sidon, no doubt in the northern district of Asher. <hi type="italic">Ebron</hi> has not yet been traced. As <hi type="italic">Abdon</hi> occurs among the towns which Asher gave up to the Levites (<reference osisRef="Josh.21.30">Jos 21:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.59">1Ch 6:59</reference>), and in this verse also twenty MSS have the reading Abdon, many writers, like <hi type="italic">Reland</hi> (Pal. p. 514), regard <hi type="italic">Ebron</hi> as a copyist’s error for <hi type="italic">Abdon</hi>. This is possible enough, but it is by no means certain. As the towns of Asher are not all given in this list, since Acco, Achlab, and Helba (Jdg 1:31) are wanting, Abdon may also have been omitted. But we cannot attach any importance to the reading of the twenty MSS, as it may easily have arisen from <reference osisRef="Josh.21.30">Jos 21:30</reference>; and in addition to the Masoretic text, it has against it the authority of all the ancient versions, in which the reading <hi type="italic">Ebron</hi> is adopted. But even <hi type="italic">Abdon</hi> cannot be traced with certainty. On the supposition that <hi type="italic">Abdon</hi> is to be read for <hi type="italic">Ebron</hi>, <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> connects it with the present <hi type="italic">Abbadiyeh</hi>, on the east of Beirut (<hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> iii. App.; <hi type="italic">Ritter</hi>, Erdk. xvii. pp. 477 and 710), or with <hi type="italic">Abidat</hi>, on the east (not the north) of Jobail (Byblus), mentioned by <hi type="italic">Burckhardt</hi> (Syr. p. 296) and <hi type="italic">Robinson</hi> (iii. App.); though he cannot adduce any other argument in support of the identity of Abdon with these two places, which are only known by name at present, except the resemblance in their names. On the supposition, however, that Abdon is not the same as Ebron, <hi type="italic">Van de Velde's</hi> conjecture is a much more natural one; namely, that it is to be found in the ruins of <hi type="italic">Abdeh</hi>, on the Wady Kurn, to the north of Acca. <hi type="italic">Rehob</hi> cannot be traced. The name occurs again in <reference osisRef="Josh.19.30">Jos 19:30</reference>, from which it is evident that there were two towns of this name in the territory of Asher (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.19.30">Jos 19:30</reference>). <hi type="italic">Schultz</hi> and <hi type="italic">Van de Velde</hi> connect it with the village of <hi type="italic">Hamûl</hi> by the wady of that name, between Ras el Abyad and Ras en Nakura; but this is too far south to be included in the district which reached to great Sidon. <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>'s suggestion would be a more probable one, namely, that it is connected with the village of <hi type="italic">Hammana</hi>, on the east of Beirut, in the district of <hi type="italic">el Metn</hi>, on the heights of Lebanon, where there is now a Maronite monastery (vid., <hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi>, i. p. 260; <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> iii. App.; and <hi type="italic">Ritter</hi>, xvii. pp. 676 and 710), if it could only be shown that the territory of Asher reached as far to the east as this. <hi type="italic">Kanah</hi> cannot be the village of <hi type="italic">Kâna</hi>, not far from Tyre (<hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> iii. p. 384), but must have been farther north, and near to Sidon, though it has not yet been discovered. For the supposition that it is connected with the existing place called <hi type="italic">Ain Kanieh</hi> (<hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> iii. App.; <hi type="italic">Ritter</hi>, xvii. pp. 94 and 703), on the north of Jezzin, is overthrown by the fact that that place is too far to the east to be thought of in this connection; and neither <hi type="italic">Robinson</hi> nor <hi type="italic">Ritter</hi> makes any allusion to “Ain <hi type="italic">Kana</hi>, in the neighbourhood of Jurjera, six hours to the south-east of Sidon,” which <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> mentions without quoting his authority, so that the existence of such a place is very questionable. On <hi type="italic">Sidon</hi>, now <hi type="italic">Saida</hi>, see at Jos 11:8.
entries.212fcd53da7ec5b09ae393b4f8c081a82aca10e0: <reference osisRef="Josh.19.33">Jos 19:33</reference> <div eID="gen2947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2948" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">Its boundary was</hi> (its territory reached) <hi type="italic">from Heleph, from the oak-forest at Zaanannim, and Adami Nekeb and Jabneel to Lakkum; and its outgoings were the Jordan</hi>.” <hi type="italic">Heleph</hi> is unknown, though in all probability it was to the south of Zaanannim, and not very far distant. According to Jdg 4:11, the <hi type="italic">oak-forest</hi> (<hi type="italic">allon</hi>: see the remarks on <reference osisRef="Gen.12.6">Gen 12:6</reference>) at <hi type="italic">Zaanannim</hi> was near <hi type="italic">Kedesh</hi>, on the north-west of Lake Huleh. There are still many oaks in that neighbourhood (<hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> Bibl. Res. p. 386); and on the south of Bint Jebail <hi type="italic">Robinson</hi> crossed a low mountain-range which was covered with small oak trees (Pal. iii. p. 372). <hi type="italic">Adami hannekeb</hi>, i.e., <hi type="italic">Adami</hi> of the pass (<hi type="italic">Nekeb</hi>, judging from the analogy of the Arabic, signifying <hi type="italic">foramen, via inter montes</hi>), is supposed by <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> to be <hi type="italic">Deir-el-ahmar</hi>, i.e., red cloister, a place which is still inhabited, three hours to the north-west of Baalbek, on the pass from the cedars to Baalbek (<hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi>, i. pp. 181, 185; <hi type="italic">Burckhardt</hi>, Syr. p. 60; and <hi type="italic">Ritter</hi>, Erdk. xvii. p. 150), so called from the reddish colour of the soil in the neighbourhood, which would explain the name <hi type="italic">Adami</hi>. <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> also connects <hi type="italic">Jabneel</hi> with the lake <hi type="italic">Jemun</hi>, <hi type="italic">Jemuni</hi>, or <hi type="italic">Jammune</hi>, some hours to the north-west of Baalbek, on the eastern side of the western Lebanon range (<hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> Bibl. Res. p. 548; <hi type="italic">Ritter</hi>, xvii. pp. 304ff.), where there are still considerable ruins of a very early date to be found, especially the ruins of an ancient temple and a celebrated place of pilgrimage, with which the name “god’s building” agrees. And lastly, he associates <hi type="italic">Lakkum</hi> with the mountains of <hi type="italic">Lokham</hi>, as the northern part of Lebanon on the Syrian mountains, from the latitude of Laodicea to that of Antioch on the western side of the Orontes, is called by the Arabian geographers <hi type="italic">Isztachri</hi>, <hi type="italic">Abulfeda</hi>, and others. So far as the names are concerned, these combinations seem appropriate enough, but they are hardly tenable. The resemblance between the names <hi type="italic">Lakkum</hi> and <hi type="italic">Lokham</hi> is only in appearance, as the Hebrew name is written with ק and the Arabic with כ. Moreover, the mountains of Lokham are much too far north for the name to be adduced as an explanation of Lakkum. The interpretation of <hi type="italic">Adami Nekeb</hi> and <hi type="italic">Jabneel</hi> is also irreconcilable with the circumstance that the lake <hi type="italic">Jamun</hi> was two hours to the west of the red convent, so that the boundary, which starts from the west, and is drawn first of all towards the north, and then to the north-east and east, must have run last of all from the red convent, and not from the Jamun lake to the Jordan. As <hi type="italic">Jabneel</hi> is mentioned after <hi type="italic">Adami Nekeb</hi>, it must be sought for to the east of Adami Nekeb, whereas the Jamun lake lies in the very opposite direction, namely, directly to the west of the red convent. The three places mentioned, therefore, cannot be precisely determined at present. The Jordan, where the boundary of Asher terminated, was no doubt the upper Jordan, or rather the <hi type="italic">Nahr Hasbany</hi>, one of the sources of the Jordan, which formed, together with the Huleh lake and the Jordan itself, between Lake Huleh and the Sea of Tiberias, and down to the point where it issues from the latter, the eastern boundary of Asher.
entries.ac258a64da9e6b5f991003c0f6df73bfcbc5d122: <reference osisRef="Josh.19.34">Jos 19:34</reference> <div eID="gen2948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2949" type="x-p"/> From the Jordan below the Lake of Tiberias, or speaking more exactly, from the point at which the Wady Bessum enters the Jordan, “<hi type="italic">the boundary</hi> (of Asher) <hi type="italic">turned westwards to Asnoth-tabor, and went thence out to Hukkok</hi>.” This boundary, i.e., the southern boundary of Asher, probably followed the course of the Wady <hi type="italic">Bessum</hi> from the Jordan, which wady was the boundary of Issachar on the north-east, and then ran most likely from <hi type="italic">Kefr Sabt</hi> (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.19.22">Jos 19:22</reference>) to <hi type="italic">Asnoth-tabor</hi>, i.e., according to the <hi type="italic">Onom.</hi> (<hi type="italic">s. v.</hi> <hi type="italic">Azanoth</hi>), a <hi type="italic">vicus ad regionem Diocaesareae pertinens in campestribus</hi>, probably on the south-east of <hi type="italic">Diocaesarea</hi>, i.e., <hi type="italic">Sepphoris</hi>, not far from Tabor, to which the boundary of Issachar extended (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.22">Jos 19:22</reference>). <hi type="italic">Hukkok</hi> has not yet been traced. <hi type="italic">Robinson</hi> (Bibl. Res. p. 82) and <hi type="italic">Van de Velde</hi> (Mem. p. 322) are inclined to follow <hi type="italic">Rabbi Parchi</hi> of the fourteenth century, and identify this place with the village of <hi type="italic">Yakûk</hi>, on the north-west of the Lake of Gennesareth; but this village is too far to the north-east to have formed the terminal point of the southern boundary of Naphtali, as it ran westwards from the Jordan. After this Naphtali touched <hi type="italic">“Zebulun on the south, Asher on the west, and Judah by the Jordan toward the sun-rising or east.”</hi> “The Jordan” is in apposition to “Judah,” in the sense of “Judah of the Jordan,” like “Jordan of Jericho” in Num 22:1; Num 26:3, etc. The Masoretic pointing, which separates these two words, was founded upon some false notion respecting this definition of the boundary, and caused the commentators great perplexity, until <hi type="italic">C. v. Raumer</hi> succeeded in removing the difficulty, by showing that the district of the sixty towns of Jair, which was upon the eastern side of the Jordan, is called Judah here, or reckoned as belonging to Judah, because Jair, the possessor of these towns, was a descendant of Judah on the father’s side through Hezron (<reference osisRef="1Chr.2.5">1Ch 2:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.21-1Chr.2.22">1Ch 2:21-22</reference>); whereas in <reference osisRef="Josh.13.30">Jos 13:30</reference>, and Num 32:41, he is reckoned <hi type="italic">contra morem</hi>, i.e., against the rule laid down in Num 36:7, as a descendant of Manasseh, on account of his descent from Machir the Manassite, on his mother’s side.<note placement="foot">See <hi type="italic">C. v. Raumer</hi>'s article on “Judaea on the east of Jordan,” in <hi type="italic">Tholuck’s litt. Anz.</hi> 1834, Nos. 1 and 2, and his Palästina, pp. 233ff. ed. 4; and for the arbitrary attempts that had been made to explain the passage by alterations of the text and in other ways, see <hi type="italic">Rosenmüller</hi>'s <hi type="italic">Bibl. Alterthk</hi>. ii. 1, pp. 301-2; and <hi type="italic">Keil's</hi> Comm. on Joshua, pp. 438-9.</note>
entries.cb963424c9bb90da6295e56cff5080bccd946a30: <reference osisRef="Josh.19.35">Jos 19:35</reference> <div eID="gen2949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2950" type="x-p"/> The fortified towns of Naphtali were the following. <hi type="italic">Ziddim:</hi> unknown, though <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> suggests that “it may possibly be preserved in <hi type="italic">Chirbet es Saudeh</hi>, to the west of the southern extremity of the Lake of Tiberias (<hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> iii. App.);” but this place is to the west of the Wady Bessum, i.e., in the territory of Issachar. <hi type="italic">Zer</hi> is also unknown. As the lxx and Syriac give the name as <hi type="italic">Zor</hi>, <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> connects it with <hi type="italic">Kerak</hi>, which signifies fortress as well as <hi type="italic">Zor</hi> (= מצור), a heap of ruins at the southern end of the lake (<hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> iii. p. 263), the place which <hi type="italic">Josephus</hi> calls Taricheae (see <hi type="italic">Reland</hi>, p. 1026), - a very doubtful combination! <hi type="italic">Hammath</hi> (i.e., <hi type="italic">thermae</hi>), a Levitical town called <hi type="italic">Hammaoth-dor</hi> in <reference osisRef="Josh.21.32">Jos 21:32</reference>, and <hi type="italic">Hammon</hi> in <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.61">1Ch 6:61</reference>, was situated, according to statements in the Talmud, somewhere near the later city of Tiberias, on the western shore of the Lake of Gennesareth, and was no doubt identical with the κώμεε Αμμαούς in the neighbourhood of Tiberias, a place with warm baths (<hi type="italic">Jos.</hi> Ant. xviii. 2, 3; Bell. Judg. iv. 1, 3). There are warm springs still to be found half an hour to the south of Tabaria, which are used as baths (<hi type="italic">Burckhardt</hi>, Syr. pp. 573-4; <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> iii. pp. 258ff.). Rakkath (according to the <hi type="italic">Talm</hi>. and <hi type="italic">Rabb. ripa littus</hi>) was situated, according to rabbinical accounts, in the immediate neighbourhood of Hammath, and was the same place as <hi type="italic">Tiberias</hi>; but the account given by <hi type="italic">Josephus</hi> (Ant. xviii. 2, 3; cf. Bell. Judg. ii. 9, 1) respecting the founding of Tiberias by Herod the tetrarch is at variance with this; so that the rabbinical statements appear to have no other foundation than the etymology of the name <hi type="italic">Rakkath</hi>. <hi type="italic">Chinnereth</hi> is given in the Targums as גניסר, גינוסר, גּנּוסר, i.e., Γεννησάρ. According to <hi type="italic">Josephus</hi> (Bell. Jud. iii. 10, 8), this name was given to a strip of land on the shore of the Sea of Galilee, which was distinguished for its natural beauty, its climate, and its fertility, namely the long plain, about twenty minutes broad and an hour long, which stretches along the western shore of this lake, from el-Mejdel on the south to Khan Minyeh on the north (<hi type="italic">Burckhardt</hi>, Syr. pp. 558-9; <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> iii. pp. 279, 290). It must have been in this plain that the town of <hi type="italic">Chinnereth</hi> stood, from which the plain and lake together derived the name of <hi type="italic">Chinnereth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.3.17">Deu 3:17</reference>) or <hi type="italic">Chinneroth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.11.2">Jos 11:2</reference>), and the lake alone the name of “Sea of Chinnereth,” or “Sea of Chinneroth” (<reference osisRef="Josh.12.3">Jos 12:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.13.27">Jos 13:27</reference>; Num 34:11).
entries.0a9593621144cdc51cf25e65ff19c694d945c919: <reference osisRef="Josh.19.36">Jos 19:36</reference> <hi type="italic">Adamah</hi> is unknown. <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> is of opinion, that as <hi type="italic">Adamah</hi> signifies red, the place referred to may possibly be <hi type="italic">Ras el Ahmar</hi>, i.e., <hi type="italic">red-head</hi>, on the north of Safed (<hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> iii. p. 370; Bibl. Res. p. 69). <hi type="italic">Ramah</hi> is the present <hi type="italic">Rameh</hi> (<hi type="italic">Ramea</hi>), a large well-built village, inhabited by Christians and Druses, surrounded by extensive olive plantations, and provided with an excellent well. It stands upon the slope of a mountain, in a beautiful plain on the south-west of Safed, but without any relics of antiquity (see <hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi>, ii. p. 129; <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> Bibl. Res. pp. 78-9). <hi type="italic">Hazor</hi> has not yet been traced with certainty (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.11.1">Jos 11:1</reference>).
entries.308291612ca7e69e0bb6eb27069666a351f57b85: <reference osisRef="Josh.19.37">Jos 19:37</reference> <hi type="italic">Kedesh</hi> (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.12.2">Jos 12:2</reference>). <hi type="italic">Edrei</hi>, a different place from the town of the same name in Bashan (<reference osisRef="Josh.1.2">Jos 1:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.1.4">Jos 1:4</reference>), is still unknown. <hi type="italic">En-hazor</hi> is probably to be sought for in <hi type="italic">Bell Hazur</hi> and <hi type="italic">Ain Hazur</hi>, which is not very far distant, on the south-west of Rameh, though the ruins upon <hi type="italic">Tell Hazur</hi> are merely the ruins of an ordinary village, with one single cistern that has fallen to pieces (<hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> Bibl. entries.64c6003a2771b6549ba893bcb7aadd85d42e2e9b: <reference osisRef="Josh.19.38-Josh.19.39">Jos 19:38-39</reference> <hi type="italic">Jireon</hi> (<hi type="italic">Iron</hi>) is probably the present village of <hi type="italic">Jarûn</hi>, an hour to the south-east of Bint-Jebeil, with the ruins of an ancient Christian church (<hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi>, ii. pp. 123-4; <hi type="italic">Van de Velde</hi>, R. i. p. 133). <hi type="italic">Migdal-el</hi>, so far as the name is concerned, might be <hi type="italic">Magdala</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.39">Mat 15:39</reference>), on the western shore of the Lake of Gennesareth, between Capernaum and Tiberias (<hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> iii. pp. 279ff.); the only difficulty is, that the towns upon this lake have already been mentioned in Jos 19:35. <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> connects <hi type="italic">Migdal-el</hi> with <hi type="italic">Chorem</hi>, so as to form one name, and finds <hi type="italic">Migdal el Chorem</hi> in the present <hi type="italic">Mejdel Kerum</hi>, on the west of Rameh (<hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi>, ii. p. 130; <hi type="italic">Van de Velde</hi>, i. p. 215), a common Mahometan village. But there is nothing to favour this combination, except the similarity in sound between the two names; whereas it has against it not only the situation of the village, which was so far to the west, being not more than three hours from Acca, that the territory of Naphtali can hardly have reached so far, but also the very small resemblance between <hi type="italic">Chorem</hi> and <hi type="italic">Kerum</hi>, not to mention the fact that the accents separate <hi type="italic">Chorem</hi> from <hi type="italic">Migdal-el</hi>, whilst the omission of the copula (<hi type="italic">vav</hi>) before <hi type="italic">Chorem</hi> cannot have any weight, as the copula is also wanting before <hi type="italic">Zer</hi> and <hi type="italic">Rakkath</hi>. <hi type="italic">Chorem</hi> and <hi type="italic">Beth-anath</hi> have not yet been discovered. From the latter place Naphtali was unable to expel the Canaanites (Jdg 1:33). <hi type="italic">Beth-shemesh</hi>, a different place from the town of the same name in Issachar (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.22">Jos 19:22</reference>), is also still unknown. The total number of towns is given as nineteen, whereas only sixteen are mentioned by name. It is hardly correct to seek for the missing places among the border towns mentioned in <reference osisRef="Josh.19.33">Jos 19:33</reference> and <reference osisRef="Josh.19.34">Jos 19:34</reference>, as the enumeration of the towns themselves is introduced by מבצר וערי in <reference osisRef="Josh.19.35">Jos 19:35</reference>, and in this way the list of towns is separated from the description of the boundaries. To this we may add, that the town of Karthan or Kirjathaim, which Naphtali gave up to the Levites (<reference osisRef="Josh.21.32">Jos 21:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.61">1Ch 6:61</reference>), does not occur either among the border towns or in the list of towns, from which we may see that the list of towns is an imperfect one. <div eID="gen2950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2951" type="x-p"/> The Inheritance of the Tribe of Dan. - This fell to the west of Benjamin, between Judah and Ephraim, and was formed by Judah giving up some of its northern towns, and Ephraim some of its southern towns, to the Danites, so as to furnish them with a territory proportionate to their number. It was situated for the most part in the lowland (<hi type="italic">shephelah</hi>), including, however, the hill country between the Mediterranean and the mountains, and extended over a portion of the plain of Sharon, so that it belonged to one of the most fruitful portions of Palestine. The boundaries are not given, because they could be traced from those of the adjoining territories.
entries.930b4d579a7cbb0e177ebe6935ab89799f796e54: <reference osisRef="Josh.19.41-Josh.19.42">Jos 19:41-42</reference> <div eID="gen2951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2952" type="x-p"/> From Judah the families of Dan received <hi type="italic">Zorea</hi> and <hi type="italic">Eshtaol</hi> (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.15.33">Jos 15:33</reference>), and <hi type="italic">Ir-shemesh</hi>, also called <hi type="italic">Beth-shemesh</hi> (1Ki 4:9), on the border of Judah (see <reference osisRef="Josh.15.10">Jos 15:10</reference>); but of these the Danites did not take possession, as they were given up by Judah to the Levites (<reference osisRef="Josh.21.16">Jos 21:16</reference> : see at <reference osisRef="Josh.15.10">Jos 15:10</reference>). <hi type="italic">Saalabbin</hi>, or <hi type="italic">Saalbim</hi>, which remained in the hands of the Canaanites (Jdg 1:35), is frequently mentioned in the history of David and Solomon (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.32">2Sa 23:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.33">1Ch 11:33</reference>; 1Ki 4:9). It may possibly be the present <hi type="italic">Selbît</hi> (<hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> iii. App.; Bibl. Res. p. 144), some distance to the north of the three places mentioned (<hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>). <hi type="italic">Ajalon</hi>, which was also not taken from the Canaanites (Jdg 1:35), was assigned to the Levites (<reference osisRef="Josh.21.24">Jos 21:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.54">1Ch 6:54</reference>). It is mentioned in the wars with the Philistines (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.31">1Sa 14:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.13">1Ch 8:13</reference>), was fortified by Rehoboam (<reference osisRef="2Chr.11.10">2Ch 11:10</reference>), and was taken by the Philistines from King Ahaz (<reference osisRef="2Chr.28.18">2Ch 28:18</reference>). It has been preserved in the village of Yalo (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.10.12">Jos 10:12</reference>). <hi type="italic">Jethlah</hi> is only mentioned here, and has not yet been discovered. So far as the name is concerned, it may possibly be preserved in the Wady <hi type="italic">Atallah</hi>, on the west of <hi type="italic">Yalo</hi> (Bibl. Res. pp. 143-4).
entries.bdb4ecf58617cd5c377efab29cce4cfad18d4ca7: <reference osisRef="Josh.19.43">Jos 19:43</reference> <hi type="italic">Elon</hi>, which is mentioned again in 1Ki 4:9, with the addition of <hi type="italic">Beth-hanan</hi>, has not yet been traced; according to <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>, it “may possibly be <hi type="italic">Ellin</hi>, near Timnath and Beth-shemesh, mentioned by <hi type="italic">Robinson</hi> in his Pal. vol. iii. App.” <hi type="italic">Thimna</hi> (<hi type="italic">Thimnathah</hi>) and <hi type="italic">Ekron</hi>, on the boundary of Judah (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.15.10-Josh.15.11">Jos 15:10-11</reference>).
entries.d7819f31ddd50dd14ad894b6b3f0f7675850cc89: <reference osisRef="Josh.19.44">Jos 19:44</reference> <hi type="italic">Eltekeh</hi> and <hi type="italic">Gibbethon</hi>, which were allotted to the Levites (<reference osisRef="Josh.21.23">Jos 21:23</reference>), have not yet been discovered. Under the earliest kings of Israel, <hi type="italic">Gibbethon</hi> was in the hands of the Philistines (1Ki 15:27; 1Ki 16:15, 1Ki 16:17). <hi type="italic">Baalath</hi> was fortified by Solomon (1Ki 9:18). According to <hi type="italic">Josephus</hi> (Ant. 8:6, 1), it was <hi type="italic">“Baleth in the neighbourhood of Geser;”</hi> probably the same place as <hi type="italic">Baalah</hi>, on the border of Judah (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.11">Jos 15:11</reference>).
entries.f5cd34944037896374206e8c2c1619eb489fc63b: <reference osisRef="Josh.19.45">Jos 19:45</reference> <hi type="italic">Jehud</hi> has probably been preserved in the village of <hi type="italic">Jehudieh</hi> (<hi type="italic">Hudieh</hi>), two hours to the north of Ludd (Diospolis), in a splendidly cultivated plain (<hi type="italic">Berggren</hi>, R. iii. p. 162; <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> iii. p. 45, and App.). <hi type="italic">Bene-berak</hi>, the present <hi type="italic">Ibn Abrak</hi>, an hour from Jehud (<hi type="italic">Scholz</hi>, R. p. 256). <hi type="italic">Gath-rimmon</hi>, which was given to the Levites (<reference osisRef="Josh.21.24">Jos 21:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.54">1Ch 6:54</reference>), is described in the <hi type="italic">Onom.</hi> (<hi type="italic">s. v.</hi>) as <hi type="italic">villa praegrandis in duodecimo milliario Diospoleos pergentibus Eleutheropolin</hi>, - a statement which points to the neighbourhood of Thimnah, though it has not yet been discovered.
entries.6a701d5168e9c860b54406b537643533c104f86b: <reference osisRef="Josh.19.46">Jos 19:46</reference> <hi type="italic">Me-jarkon</hi>, i.e., <hi type="italic">aquae flavedinis</hi>, and <hi type="italic">Rakkon</hi>, are unknown; but from the clause which follows, <hi type="italic">“with the territory before Japho,”</hi> it must have been in the neighbourhood of Joppa (Jaffa). “The territory before Japho” includes the places in the environs of Joppa. Consequently <hi type="italic">Joppa</hi> itself does not appear to have belonged to the territory of Dan, although, according to Jdg 5:17, the Danites must have had possession of this town. <hi type="italic">Japho</hi>, the well-known port of Palestine (<reference osisRef="2Chr.2.15">2Ch 2:15</reference>; Ezr 3:7; <reference osisRef="Jonah.1.3">Jon 1:3</reference>), which the Greeks called Ἰόππη (Joppa), the present <hi type="italic">Jaffa</hi> (see <hi type="italic">v. Raumer</hi>, Pal. pp. 204-5, and <hi type="italic">Ritter</hi>, Erdk. xvi. pp. 574ff.).
entries.8cd2b66a8270e33b2ac112882cccb3670531ac81: <reference osisRef="Josh.19.47-Josh.19.48">Jos 19:47-48</reference> <div eID="gen2952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2953" type="x-p"/> Besides this inheritance, the Danites of Zorea and Eshtaol went, after Joshua’s death, and conquered the town of <hi type="italic">Leshem</hi> or <hi type="italic">Laish</hi>, on the northern boundary of Canaan, and gave it the name of <hi type="italic">Dan</hi>, as the territory which was allotted to them under Joshua was too small for them, on account of their inability to drive out the Amorites from several of their towns (Jdg 1:34-35; Jdg 18:2). For further particulars concerning this conquest, see Judg 18. <hi type="italic">Leshem</hi> or <hi type="italic">Laish</hi> (Jdg 18:7, Jdg 18:27), i.e., <hi type="italic">Dan</hi>, which the <hi type="italic">Onom.</hi> describes as <hi type="italic">viculus quarto a Paneade milliario euntibus Tyrum</hi>, was the present <hi type="italic">Tell el Kadi</hi>, or <hi type="italic">el Leddan</hi>, the central source of the Jordan, to the west of Banjas, a place with ancient ruins (see <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> iii. p. 351; Bibl. Res. pp. 390, 393). It was there that Jeroboam set up the golden calves (1Ki 12:29-30, etc.); and it is frequently mentioned as the northernmost city of the Israelites, in contrast with Beersheba, which was in the extreme south of the land (Jdg 20:1; <reference osisRef="1Sam.3.20">1Sa 3:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.10">2Sa 3:10</reference> : see also <hi type="italic">Ritter</hi>, Erdk. xvi. pp. 207ff.).<hi type="italic">Conclusion of the Distribution of the Land</hi>. - <reference osisRef="Josh.19.49">Jos 19:49</reference>, Jos 19:50. When the land was distributed among the tribes according to its territories, the Israelites gave Joshua an inheritance in the midst of them, according to the command of Jehovah, namely the town of <hi type="italic">Timnath-serah</hi>, upon the mountains of Ephraim, for which he asked, and which he finished building; and there he dwelt until the time of his death (<reference osisRef="Josh.24.30">Jos 24:30</reference>; Jdg 2:9). <hi type="italic">“According to the word of the Lord”</hi> (lit. “at the mouth of Jehovah”) does not refer to a divine oracle communicated through the high priest, but to a promise which Joshua had probably received from God at the same time as Caleb, viz., in Kadesh, but which, like the promise given to Caleb, is not mentioned in the Pentateuch (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.15.13">Jos 15:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.14.9">Jos 14:9</reference>). <hi type="italic">Timnath-serah</hi>, called <hi type="italic">Timnath-heres</hi> in Jdg 2:9, must not be confounded with <hi type="italic">Timnah</hi> in the tribe of Dan (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.43">Jos 19:43</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.15.10">Jos 15:10</reference>), as is the case in the <hi type="italic">Onom.</hi> It has been preserved in the present ruins and foundation walls of a place called <hi type="italic">Tibneh</hi>, which was once a large town, about seven hours to the north of Jerusalem, and two hours to the west of Jiljilia, standing upon two mountains, with many caverns that have been used as graves (see <hi type="italic">Eli Smith</hi> in <hi type="italic">Ritter</hi>, Erdk. xvi. pp. 562ff., and <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> Bibl. Res. p. 141).
entries.827eb2814d569b94c8193cc9cf19b86359f65671: <reference osisRef="Josh.19.51">Jos 19:51</reference> <div eID="gen2953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2954" type="x-p"/> Closing formula to the account of the distribution of the land, which refers primarily to Jos 18:1., as the expression “<hi type="italic">in Shiloh</hi>” shows, but which also includes Josh 14-17. The Preamble - <reference osisRef="Josh.1.1-Josh.1.9">Jos 1:1-9</reference> <div eID="gen2954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2955" type="x-p"/> After the death of Moses the Lord summoned Joshua, the servant of Moses, whom He had appointed as the leader of Israel into Canaan, to go with all the people across the Jordan, and take the land which had been promised to the fathers on oath, assuring him at the same time of His powerful aid, on condition that he observed the law of Moses faithfully. This summons and promise of God form the preamble to the whole book, which is linked on to the conclusion of the Pentateuch by the introductory words, “And it came to pass after the death of Moses, the servant of the Lord,” though it is not so closely connected as to warrant the conclusion that the two works have been written by the same author.  <chapter eID="Josh.19"/> <div eID="gen2955" type="x-p"/>

entries.6a83d0d7cb6f4917d38b3337e80dec4e336f6185: <div annotateRef="Bible:Josh.19.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Josh.19.1" sID="gen24224" type="section"/> <div sID="gen24225" type="x-p"/>Next followed the lot of the tribe of Simeon, not as a mark of honor, but rather as a mark of disgrace. Jacob had declared with regard to Simeon and Levi, “I will divide them in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.49.7">Genesis 49:7</reference>) The punishment of Levi, indeed, was not only mitigated, but converted into an excellent dignity, inasmuch as his posterity were placed on a kind of watch-towers to keep the people in the paths of piety. In regard to Simeon, the dispersion of which Jacob prophesied, manifestly took place when certain cities within the territory of Judah were assigned to his posterity for their inheritance. For although they were not sent off to great distances, yet they dwelt dispersed, and as strangers in a land properly belonging to another. Therefore, on account of the slaughter which they had perpetrated with no less perfidy than cruelty, they were placed separately in different abodes. In this way the guilt of the father was visited upon his children, and the Lord ratified in fact that sentence which he had dictated to his servant. The truth of the lot also was clearly proven.<div eID="gen24225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24226" type="x-p"/>In the circumstance of a certain portion being withdrawn from the family of Judah, we again perceive that though the dividers had carefully endeavored to observe equity, they had fallen into error, which they were not ashamed to correct as soon as it was discovered. And though they were guided by the Spirit, there is nothing strange in their having been partially mistaken, because God sometimes leaves his servants destitute of the spirit of judgment, and suffers them to act like men on different occasions, that they may not plume themselves too much on their clear-sightedness. We may add that the people were punished for their carelessness and confident haste, because they ought at the outset to have ascertained more accurately how much land could be properly assigned to each. This they neglected to do. Through their unskillful procedure, the children of Judah had received a disproportion accumulation of territory, and equity required that they should relinquish a part. It would also have been better for themselves to have their limits fixed with certainty at once than to be subjected to a galling spoliation afterwards. Add that each tribe had indulged the vain hope that its members would dwell far and wide, as if the land had been of unlimited extent.<div eID="gen24226" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Josh.19.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen24224" osisID="Josh.19.1" type="section"/>
entries.f9bfb33686891b55141678f13246dc60ae1f0d52:
9. Out of the portion of the children of Judah, etc The praise of moderation is due to the tribe of Judah for not contending that the abstraction of any part of the inheritance already assigned to them was unjust. They might easily have obtruded the name of God, and asserted that it was only by his authority they had obtained that settlement. But as it is decided by the common consent of all the tribes that more has been given to them than they can possess without loss and injury to the others, they immediately desist from all pretext for disputing the matter. And it is certain that if they had alleged the authority of God, it would have been falsely and wickedly, inasmuch as though their lot had been determined by him in regard to its situation, an error had taken place with regard to its extent, their limits having been fixed by human judgment wider than they ought. Therefore, acknowledging that it would have been wrong to give them what would occasion loss to others, they willingly resign it, and give a welcome reception to their brethren, who must otherwise have remained without inheritance, nay, submit to go shares with them in that which they supposed they had acquired beyond controversy.
Joshua 19:10-31
10. And the third lot came up for the children of Zebulun according to their families: and the border of their inheritance was unto Sarid:
10. Ascendit autem sors tertia filiis Zabulon per familias suas: et fuit terminus haereditatis eorum usque ad Sarid.
11. And their border went up toward the sea, and Maralah, and reached to Dabbasheth, and reached to the river that is before Jokneam;
11. Ascenditque terminus eorum ad mare: et Maralah, et pertingit ad Dabbaseth: pervenitque ad flumen quod est e regione Jocneam.
12. And turned from Sarid eastward toward the sunrising unto the border of Chislothtabor, and then goeth out to Daberath, and goeth up to Japhia,
12. Revertiturque a Sarid ad orientem, id est, ad ortum solis, ad terminum Chisloth-Thabor, et illinc egreditur ad Dobrath, et ascendit in Japhia.
13. And from thence passes on along on the east to Gittahhepher, to Ittahkazin, and goeth out to Remmonmethoar to Neah;
13. Inde praeterea transit ad orientem, ad ortum, ad Githah-Hepher, et ad Ihtah-casin: et illinc exit in Rimmon, et gyrat ad Neah:

14. Gyrat item idem terminus ab aquilone ad Hannathon: suntque egressus ejus ad vallem Iphthael.
15. And Kattath, and Nahallal, and Shimron, and Idalah, and Bethlehem: twelve cities with their villages.
15. Et Catthath, et Nahalal, et Simron, et Idalah, et Bethlehem: urbes duodecim, et villae earum.
16. This is the inheritance of the children of Zebulun according to their families, these cities with their villages.
16. Haec est haereditas filiorum Zabulon per familias suas: urbes istae, et villae earum.
17. And the fourth lot came out to Issachar, for the children of Issachar according to their families.
17. Ipsi Issachar egressa est sors quarta, filiis inquam, Issachar per familias suas.
18. And their border was toward Jezreel, and Chesulloth, and Shunem,
18. Et fuit terminus eorum Jezrael, et Chesuloth, et Sunem,
19. And Hapharaim, and Shion, and Anaharath,
19. Et Hapharaim, et Sion, et Anaharath,

entries.5a143408ef3ad0f7e03b6e8560229637ab421503: <div annotateRef="Bible:Josh.19.10" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Josh.19.10" sID="gen24276" type="section"/> <div sID="gen24277" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">10.</hi> <hi type="italic">And the third lot came up, </hi>etc In the lot of Zebulun there is a clear fulfillment of the prophecy of Jacob, which had foretold that they would dwell on the sea-coast. An old man, an exile who could not set a foot on his own land, <note n="168"> <div sID="gen24278" type="x-p"/> French, “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Estant un vieillard, povre banni, qui n’avoit pas un pied de terre a luy ou il peust marcher</foreign>;” “Being an old man, a poor exile, who had not a foot of land of his own on which he could walk.” — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen24278" type="x-p"/> </note> assigned a maritime district to the posterity of his son Zebulun. What could be more extravagant? But now, when the lot assigns them a maritime region, no clearer confirmation of his decision could be desired. It was just as if God were twice thundering from heaven. The tribe of Zebulun, therefore, do not occupy the shore of their own accord or by human suffrage, but a divine arrangement fixes their habitation contiguous to the sea. Thus, although men erred, still the light was always seen shining brightly in the darkness. Jacob goes farther, and makes a clear distinction between Zebulun and Issachar. The former tribe will travel far and wide, carrying on trade and commerce; the latter remaining in his tents, will cultivate ease and a sedentary life. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.49.13-Gen.49.15">Genesis 49:13-15</reference>) Hence it is probable that the sea-coast where Zebulun settled, was provided with harbors and well adapted for the various forms of commercial intercourse, <note n="169"> <div sID="gen24279" type="x-p"/> The extent of coast possessed by Zebulun was of very limited extent, but included the large and beautiful bay of Acre, which commences in the north at the promontory on which the town of Acre stands, and is terminated magnificently in the south by the lofty heights of Mount Carmel. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen24279" type="x-p"/> </note> whereas the children of Issachar were contented with their own produce, and consumed the fruits which they had raised by their own labor and culture at home.<div eID="gen24277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24280" type="x-p"/>Those who are thought to be well acquainted with these countries, affirm that the land of the tribe of Asher was fertile in corn. <note n="170"> <div sID="gen24281" type="x-p"/> The greater part of it consisted of a rich and undulating plain, diversified by gentle hills, well watered by the Leontes and other streams which derived their supplies from the snowy heights of Lebanon, and sloping gradually to that part of the sea-coast, on which were built the famous cities of Tyre and Sidon. According to Clarke, the plain of Asher and Zebulun bore a considerable resemblance to the southern districts of England. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen24281" type="x-p"/> </note> This is in complete accordance both with the letter and the spirit of Jacob’s prophecy. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.49.20">Genesis 49:20</reference>) From the fact that only a small number of cities are designated by name, we may infer that there were then many ruined cities which were not taken into account, and from the other fact that the people dwelt commodiously, we may also infer that they built many cities, with which it is plain from other passages that the land was adorned. And it is certainly apparent that only a summary of the division is briefly glanced at, and that thus many things were omitted which no religious feeling forbids us to investigate, provided we do not indulge in an excessive curiosity leading to no beneficial result. There cannot be a doubt that those to whom twenty or even only seventeen cities are attributed, had more extensive territories. Therefore, all we have here is a compendious description of the division as it was taken from the general and confused notes of the surveyors.<div eID="gen24280" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Josh.19.10" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen24276" osisID="Josh.19.10" type="section"/>

The next lot mentioned is that of Naphtali, and it seems to correspond with the disposition and manners of that tribe. For Jacob had testified, Naphtali is a hind let loose; he gave goodly words. For this reason they seem to have been contiguous on one side to the children of Judah, and to have been surrounded on other sides by the enclosures of their brethren.
The tribe of Naphtali, as marked out by Joshua, Eleazar, and the heads of the tribes, harmonizes well with the figurative description of it given by Jacob, for both in scenery and fertility it is one of the fairest in the Promised Land, but the locality assigned to it in the Commentary is singularly inaccurate. In the Latin it is said that the children of Naphtali “Videntur contigui ab una parte fuisse filiis Juda: alibi autem cincti coste ils estoyent contigus aux enfans de Juda; et d’autrepart qu’ils estoyent environnez du secours de leurs freres;” “It seems that on one side that they were surrounded by the help of their brethren.” The fact, however, is that Judah and Naphtali are at the opposite extremities of the country, and so far from being contiguous to each other, are widely separated by the intervention of no fewer than five tribes, which commencing on the frontiers of Judah, and proceeding northwards, are, in succession, Benjamin, Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar, and Zebulun. Then, as it stretched from the shores of the lake of Gennesaret, north to the roots of Lebanon, it cannot well be said to have been surrounded on all sides by the enclosures of other tribes. It certainly had Zebulun on the south-west, and Asher on the west, but on the north and east, it formed the extreme frontiers of the Promised Land, and, of course, bounded with foreign and hostile settlements. — Ed.
Indeed, in its being said that the tribe of Dan took Lesen, there seems to be a tacit comparison, because the children of Naphtali did not employ arms to force their way into their inheritance, but kept themselves quietly in a subdued territory, and thus enjoyed safety and tranquillity under the faith, and, as it were, protection of Judah and the other tribes. The capture of Lesen by the children of Dan, in accordance with the divine grant which they had received of it, did not take place till after the death of Joshua. But the fact which is more fully detailed in the book of Judges is here mentioned in passing, because praise was due to them for their boldness and activity in thus embracing the right which God had bestowed upon them, and so trusting in him as to go down bravely and defeat the enemy.

49. When they had made an end of dividing, etc We have here, at length, an account of the gratitude of the people towards Joshua. For although the partition of the land of Canaan, among the posterity of Abraham, behooved to be equitable, yet Joshua, by his excellent virtues, deserved some honorary reward. Nor could any complain that a single individual was enriched at their expense. For, first, in the delay there was a striking proof of the moderation of this holy servant of God. He does not give any heed to his own interest till the commonweal has been secured. How seldom do we find any who, after they have given one or two specimens of valor, do not forthwith make haste to the prey? Not so Joshua, who thinks not of himself till the land has been divided. In the reward itself also the same temperance and frugality are conspicuous. The city he asks to be given to himself and his family was a mere heap of stones, either because it had been demolished and converted into a heap of ruins, or because no city had yet been built upon it.
It is conjectured with probability, that with the view of making the grant as little invidious as possible, the city he requested was of no great value. If any one thinks it strange that he did not give his labor gratuitously, let him reflect that Joshua liberally obeyed the divine call, and had no mercenary feelings in undergoing so many labors, dangers, and troubles; but having spontaneously performed his duty, he behooved not to repudiate a memorial of the favor of God, unless he wished by perverse contempt to suppress his glory. For the grant voted to him was nothing else than a simple testimonial of the divine power, which had been manifested through his hand. Truly no ambition can be detected here, inasmuch as he desires nothing for himself, and does not rashly act from a feeling of covetousness, but seeks in the popular consent a confirmation of the honor which God had already bestowed upon him. To have been silent in such a case, would have been more indicative of heartlessness than of modesty. The statement in the concluding verse of the chapter, that Joshua and Eleazar made an end of dividing the land, points to the perpetuity of the boundaries, which had been fixed, and warns the children of Israel against moving in any way to unsettle an inviolable decree.
CHAPTER 20
Joshua 20:1-9

1. Loquutus est autem Jehova ad Josue, dicendo,
